body.text: NASA's Crew-12 astronauts are set to parachute back to Earth in a SpaceX capsule after 237 days of orbital research and lab maintenance on the International Space Station.
The four crew members launched into space on February 13 to oversee scientific investigations to help prepare humans for future Moon and Mars exploration, the US space agency said.
Preparations for their return have been underway for several weeks, and the astronauts' SpaceX Dragon capsule undocked from the ISS on Wednesday evening, Australian time.
Here is what to know about their expected splashdown voyage.
When will NASA SpaceX Crew-12 return to Earth?
The astronauts have already started their 27-hour voyage home and are currently in orbital transit.

NASA said the quartet's return began with the closure of the Dragon capsule's hatch at 6:05am US Eastern time (8:05pm AEST) on Wednesday, followed by a final undocking from the ISS at 8:05am (10:05pm AEST).
The timeline of their expected descent and splashdown into the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California is:
• 10:20am EDT Thursday (12:20am AEST Friday): NASA begins voyage live coverage;
• 10:46am EDT Thursday (12:46am AEST Friday): SpaceX Dragon capsule begins deorbit burn and controlled descent;
• 11:34am EDT Thursday (1:34am AEST Friday): Splashdown, followed by a NASA and SpaceX crew retrieval.
The US space agency said the crew have spent weeks packing items to return with them to Earth, including personal belongings, cargo and scientific samples.
During their descent to Earth, the astronauts will need to drink fluids from bags containing salt tablets to maintain hydration and help their bodies adjust to a return to gravity, NASA said.
Who are the Crew-12 astronauts?

The astronaut crew consists of NASA's Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, serving as the mission's commander and pilot respectively, as well as French engineer and specialist helicopter pilot Sophie Adenot and Russian military pilot and cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev.
This latest mission was Commander Meir's second in space since being selected as a NASA astronaut in 2013.
During her first voyage, she spent 205 days in orbit as a flight engineer and took part in NASA's first three all-woman spacewalks outside the ISS.
US Navy Commander Hathaway became a NASA astronaut in 2021 and this year's mission was his first in space.
Beforehand, he was deployed aboard the USS Harry S Truman aircraft carrier and accumulated more than 2,500 flight hours in 30 different aircraft, including 39 combat missions.
This mission was also the first for French Air Force Colonel Adenot, who previously worked as an Airbus helicopter cockpit design engineer, search and rescue pilot and formation flight leader.
Roscosmos cosmonaut and Air Force Major Fedyaev was previously deployed to the ISS for 186 days in 2023 as a mission specialist for NASA's SpaceX Crew-6.
Before that, he was a military pilot engineer and served in the Russian Ilyushin-38 aircraft unit in the Kamchatka Region.
What did Crew-12 work on?
The 12th SpaceX rotation voyage to the ISS was aimed at research and technology advancements "for future Moon and Mars missions and [to] benefit humanity back on Earth", NASA said.
The astronauts' research included:
• Studies of pneumonia-causing bacteria to improve potential treatments;
• On-demand intravenous fluid generation for future missions;
• The monitoring of plant health and enhanced microbe food production in space, and;
• Examinations of how a person's physical characteristics could affect blood flow during spaceflight.
Support teams aboard the ISS also helped Crew-12 prepare a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket booster for a second flight.
Who replaced Crew-12 in space?
The four astronauts taking the place of Crew-12 aboard the ISS arrived in space on October 1 after an eight-hour express rocket launch into orbit that set a US speed record.
Crew-13 is being led by NASA flight engineer Jessica Watkins — a geologist and the first Black woman to command a crew into orbit.
She will be joined by NASA’s Luke Delaney, who is a retired Marine; Canada’s Joshua Kutryk, a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force; and Russia’s Sergey Teteryatnikov, a former submariner.
Colonel Kutryk will become the fourth man to become a father while orbiting Earth, with his wife Heather due to give birth to their third child in late November.
Their stay on the ISS will last six months, but the four astronauts have already begun their work.

NASA said in their first days in space, Commander Watkins collected and analysed her own blood samples for a risk assessment study of space-caused blood clots, while Major Delaney logged his sleep patterns to monitor his health data.

Colonel Kutryk had his veins scanned by a device used on the ISS to monitor cardiovascular health, and cosmonaut Teteryatnikov wore an acoustic sensor around his neck to record his breathing for a respiratory study.
What is the ISS?
First launched in November 1988, the ISS became a continuous, inhabitable space base for humanity in the year 2000.

NASA describes it as "the most enduring platform for international cooperation in orbit", and the temporary home of flight crews from various nations, inter-orbital missions, launch vehicles, training and engineering facilities and communications networks.
Its primary use is for research on living and working in space, with the ultimate goal of allowing humans to be sent further into space than ever before.
The ISS orbits Earth at a speed of about 28,163km/h, meaning it laps the planet roughly every 90 minutes.
The main ground control centres that oversee operations aboard the ISS are located in the US and Russia, however there are also additional support centres in Canada, Japan and Europe.

While the expected life span of the ISS has been extended multiple times, the entire base exists as separate, connected modules — meaning when one part wears out or becomes unusable, it can be replaced.
NASA says the station should be able to remain a working laboratory until at least 2030.
ABC/AP
